newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-No wage cuts in Australia job sharing -Oppn.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-No wage cuts in Australia job sharing -Oppn.

text.p: Australian Opposition employment spokesman Martin Ferguson, advocating job sharing, said on the policy would not cut wages or employment conditions.
"It's not about cutting wages, it's not about cutting conditions of employment," Ferguson told Australian Broadcasting Corp television.
"This is about workers sitting down and working out what package, including shorter hours and increased leisure, suits their needs and the needs of their employer," he said.
It would be an appropriate option in the teaching service, the vehicle industry and in other factories and workplaces, he said.

But a 1993 report prepared by the previous Labor government said that job sharing might increase employment in the short term but cost jobs in the long term because of lower productivity, which would be reflected in incomes.

"In fact, the experience of countries which have reduced working hours or who encourage early retirement tends to support the view that these policies are more likely to lead to higher and more entrenched unemployment," it said.
It found reductions in working time led to declines in employment. Employers eventually had to offer disproportionately large financial incentives to sustain job sharing.
"In practice deliberately limiting work hours and working lives can reduce the level of output and make the cake smaller."
Growth prospects could be restrained by inflexibilities in the economy, increase capacity constraints and inflationary pressures, the 1993 report said.
Australian unemployment reached a 1930s post-depression record of 11.0 percent in 1992. It fell rapidly after that but stopped falling in 1995 at 8.4 percent.
The trend rate has crept up since than to reach 8.7 percent in December.
